loanable-funds-s1.title: A loanable funds market after a shift

loanable-funds-s2.title: Saving in the invented country of Brin

table.caption: Yearly saving and the government's accounts in Brin, in billions of dollars (invented data for practice).

loanable-funds-s3.title: A new savings plan in Lorne
loanable-funds-s3.text: The invented country of Lorne starts a retirement savings plan that lets households keep more of the interest they earn. Households respond by saving a larger share of their income. Nothing else changes.

items.q: The graph shows the demand for loanable funds shifting right. Which event could have caused it?
options: Households decide to save more of their income
The real interest rate falls
The government borrows more to pay for new spending
Firms expect lower profits from new equipment

why.correct: The demand for loanable funds comes from borrowers: firms that invest, households and the government.
options: More saving shifts the supply of loanable funds right, not demand.
A change in the real interest rate moves along the curves; it does not shift them.
Right: government borrowing adds to the demand for loanable funds.
Gloomier firms borrow less, which shifts demand left.

items.q: In the graph, what happens to the equilibrium real interest rate?
options: It rises
It falls
It stays the same
It falls, then returns

why.correct: A rise in the demand for loanable funds raises the real interest rate and the quantity of loanable funds.
options: Right: more demand for a given supply of loanable funds raises their price, the real interest rate.
A rightward shift of demand along upward-sloping supply raises the rate.
The demand shift moves the equilibrium up along the supply curve.
The new equilibrium stays at the higher rate while the shift lasts.

items.q: Suppose the shift in the graph came from more government borrowing. What happens to the amount private firms borrow for investment?
options: It rises, because more funds are lent in total
It does not change, because firms' demand did not shift
It falls, because the real interest rate is higher
It rises, because the government is spending more

why.correct: Government borrowing raises the real interest rate, and the higher rate lowers the quantity of private investment.
options: More is lent in total, but the government takes a bigger share at a higher real rate.
Firms' demand did not shift, but the higher real rate moves them along it to less borrowing.
Right: at the higher real rate, some private investment projects no longer pay off.
Government spending does not lower firms' borrowing costs; the higher real rate raises them.

items.q: In the graph, what happens to the quantity of loanable funds?
options: It falls, because the real interest rate rose
It stays the same, because saving did not change
It rises, as savers lend more at the higher rate
It is not shown on the graph

why.correct: When demand shifts right along an upward-sloping supply curve, both the real interest rate and the quantity rise.
options: A higher rate cuts borrowing along the old demand, but here demand shifted right.
Saving rises along the supply curve as the real rate rises.
Right: the higher real rate draws out more saving, a movement along supply.
One curve shifted, so both changes are clear: the rate and the quantity rise.

items.q: What is public saving in Brin, in billions of dollars?

why.correct: Public saving = tax revenue - government spending = 900 - 1,000 = -100 billion. The government spends more than it collects.

mistakes.why: The size is right, but the government spends more than it collects, so public saving is negative: -100.
Public saving is revenue minus spending, not their sum.

items.q: What is national saving in Brin, in billions of dollars?

why.correct: National saving = private saving + public saving = 400 + (-100) = 300 billion.

mistakes.why: You added 100 instead of -100. Public saving is negative here, so it lowers national saving.
400 is private saving alone. Add public saving, which is -100.

items.q: What does Brin's public saving tell you about the loanable funds market?
options: The government adds \$100 billion to the supply of loanable funds
The government has to borrow \$100 billion, adding to the demand for loanable funds
The government plays no part, since private saving is what counts
Households have to save \$100 billion less

why.correct: When public saving is negative, the government borrows, which adds to the demand for loanable funds (or, put the other way, lowers national saving).
options: Public saving is negative, so the government takes funds out rather than adding them.
Right: it spends \$100 billion more than it collects and borrows the difference.
Government borrowing and saving are part of the market.
Private saving is given as 400; it is the government that borrows.

items.q: Brin raises taxes so that tax revenue equals government spending, and private saving stays at 400. What happens to national saving and the real interest rate?
options: National saving falls and the real rate rises
National saving rises to 400 and the real rate falls
Both are unchanged, since private saving is the same
National saving rises and the real rate rises

why.correct: Less government borrowing means more national saving and a lower real interest rate.
options: Public saving rises from -100 to 0, so national saving rises, not falls.
Right: with no government borrowing, there is less demand for loanable funds, so the real rate falls.
Public saving changed from -100 to 0, so national saving changes.
Less government borrowing lowers the real interest rate.

items.q: On the loanable funds graph, show the effect of Lorne's savings plan and mark the new equilibrium.

why.correct: More household saving shifts the supply of loanable funds right, so the real interest rate falls and the quantity of loanable funds rises.

slips.DLF: Saving is the source of loanable funds, so more saving shifts supply, not demand.

items.q: After the savings plan, what happens to business investment in Lorne?
options: It rises, because the real interest rate falls
It falls, because households spend less
It does not change, because firms' demand did not shift
It falls, because the real interest rate rises

why.correct: More saving lowers the real interest rate, so the quantity of loanable funds borrowed for investment rises.
options: Right: cheaper borrowing makes more investment projects worth doing.
The loanable funds market shows the lower real rate raising investment.
Demand did not shift, but the lower real rate moves firms along it to more borrowing.
More saving lowers the real interest rate.

items.q: In the scenario, who supplies loanable funds?
options: Firms that want to build factories
Households that save part of their income
The central bank, by setting the policy rate
Stores that sell goods to households

why.correct: Savers supply loanable funds; borrowers, such as investing firms and a government that spends more than it collects, demand them.
options: Firms that invest are borrowers: the demand side.
Right: saving is the supply of loanable funds.
The loanable funds market is about saving and borrowing; the policy rate is another graph.
Selling goods is not lending; savers supply loanable funds.

items.q: At a real interest rate below the equilibrium rate, firms want to borrow more. Label the axes and curves of the loanable funds graph, then mark point C on the demand curve at a real interest rate below equilibrium.

why.correct: Loanable funds: the real interest rate (vertical) and the quantity of loanable funds (horizontal), DLF sloping down and SLF up. Along DLF a lower real rate means more borrowing, so C sits down and to the right of the equilibrium.

items.q: Firms become more optimistic about the profits from new equipment. Shift the right curve and mark the new equilibrium.

why.correct: More planned investment means more borrowing at each real rate: the demand for loanable funds shifts right, raising the real interest rate and the quantity of loanable funds.

key.because: a rise in planned investment by firms

slips.SLF: Optimistic firms want to borrow more, which is the demand for loanable funds. Supply comes from savers.

items.q: Mark point B on the supply of loanable funds curve at a real interest rate above the equilibrium rate.

why.correct: Along SLF, a higher real interest rate draws out more saving, so B sits up and to the right of the equilibrium.

items.q: What goes on the vertical axis of the loanable funds graph?
options: The nominal interest rate
The real interest rate
The price level
The quantity of loanable funds

why.correct: Loanable funds: real interest rate (r) on the vertical axis. Writing "nominal" loses the graph point.
options: The nominal rate goes on the money market graph. Saving and borrowing decisions depend on the real rate.
Right: savers and borrowers care about the return and cost after inflation.
The price level goes on the AD-AS graph.
That goes on the horizontal axis.

items.q: Which of these shift the demand for loanable funds to the right? Select all that apply.
options: The government borrows more to cover its spending
Firms expect lower returns on new investment
Households save a larger share of their income
The real interest rate falls

why.correct: Demand for loanable funds shifts with borrowing plans: government borrowing and firms' expected returns on investment.
options: Right: the government becomes a bigger borrower.
Gloomier firms borrow less at each real rate, a shift to the left.
More saving shifts supply right, not demand.
That is a movement along demand, not a shift.

items.q: Why does the supply of loanable funds slope upward?
options: A higher real interest rate rewards saving, so people save and lend more
Banks are required to lend more when rates rise
Inflation rises as the real interest rate rises
The government saves more when rates rise

why.correct: Saving responds to the reward for saving, the real interest rate: a higher rate brings out more loanable funds.
options: Right: the real rate is the reward for saving.
No rule makes banks lend more; savers choose to supply more at higher rates.
The real rate already removes inflation; the slope comes from savers' choices.
Public saving depends on taxes and spending, not on the slope of supply.

items.q: Put the links in order, from more government borrowing to private investment.
options: The government borrows more
The demand for loanable funds shifts right
The real interest rate rises
Borrowing costs rise for firms
The quantity of private investment falls

why.correct: Government borrowing raises the real interest rate, and the higher rate lowers private investment.

items.q: Make it specific: explain how more government borrowing affects private investment.

why.correct: Government borrowing raises the demand for loanable funds, the real interest rate rises, and private investment falls because borrowing costs more.

specific.frame: The government borrows more, so the ___ for loanable funds shifts ___; the real interest rate ___, so private investment ___.
specific.model: The government borrows more, so the demand for loanable funds shifts right; the real interest rate increases, so private investment decreases because borrowing becomes more costly for firms.

curve.label: Which curve
options: demand
supply

why.1: The government is a borrower here, so it adds to demand. (Showing lower national saving as supply shifting left also raises the rate.)

direction.label: Which way
options: right
left

why.1: More borrowing at each rate is a shift to the right.

rate.label: The real interest rate
options: rises
falls

why.1: More demand for the same supply raises the real rate.

spending.label: Private investment
options: falls
rises

why.1: A higher real rate makes borrowing for investment costlier, so it falls.
